overview: Edward II was king of England from 1307 to 1327. His defeat at Bannockburn and later deposition made his reign a crisis point in Plantagenet monarchy.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Edward II was king of England from 1307 to 1327. His defeat at Bannockburn and later deposition made his reign a crisis point in Plantagenet monarchy.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Edward II of England was born 1284, associated with Caernarfon Castle. The early evidence is uneven, so precise details should be treated carefully.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Edward II of England is remembered as one of medieval England's most disastrous kings, and the sources are nearly unanimous in presenting a ruler whose personal favouritism and political ineptitude destroyed him. Chroniclers, largely hostile, dwell on his devotion to favourites — first Piers Gaveston, later the Despensers — whose elevation enraged the baronage and drained royal authority, and on his lack of interest in the martial kingship his barons expected.

They also record his humiliating defeat by Robert the Bruce at the Battle of Bannockburn, his inability to manage the great magnates, and the descent of his reign into civil conflict, ending in his deposition and murder. The sources note, sometimes with disapproval, his fondness for rustic pastimes unbecoming a king, and his emotional attachment to his favourites above his nobles and queen.

The portrait is shaped by the contempt of chroniclers writing after his fall, so the personal failings are emphasised to explain the catastrophe. What the record consistently conveys is a ruler who inspired loyalty in a narrow circle and alienation in almost everyone else — remembered as devoted, stubborn, and politically calamitous, a king undone by misjudged affections and incapacity to rule.

contentSections.title: As king of England
paragraphs: Edward struggled with aristocratic opposition, controversial favorites, and war in Scotland. At Bannockburn, his army failed against Robert the Bruce’s disciplined Scottish forces.
Battle of Bannockburn gives Edward II of England's career a specific military and political setting: his choices, command, defeat, or death affected the outcome remembered in that article.

contentSections.title: Death
paragraphs: Died in captivity at Berkeley Castle in 1327 after deposition; the exact manner of death remains disputed.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Edward II’s reign became a warning example of political failure, noble opposition, and the limits of royal authority. His defeat at Bannockburn, conflict with the Ordainers, dependence on favorites, deposition in 1327, and death in captivity gave later writers a dramatic case of kingship undone by mistrust and misrule.

keyAchievements.title: Ruled England from 1307
keyAchievements.description: Edward inherited his father’s Scottish war and a kingdom strained by aristocratic opposition.

keyAchievements.title: Led the English army at Bannockburn
keyAchievements.description: At Bannockburn, Edward’s army failed to use its size effectively and collapsed against Bruce’s schiltrons.

keyAchievements.title: His deposition reshaped royal politics
keyAchievements.description: His forced abdication in 1327 became a major precedent for removing an anointed king.
